kunyah: Abu Musa — his name was Abdullah ibn Qays
teaser: The Prophet ﷺ compared his voice to the mizmars of Dawud's family. He never knew he was being listened to.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A Yemeni who arrived with nothing but his tribe
layers.content:
His name was 'Abdullah ibn Qays, of the Ash'ar, a tribe of Yemen. Almost everyone called him by his kunya: Abu Musa.

The sources are close to silent about his childhood. There is no famous story of his youth in Yemen, no account of his trade before Islam, no description of his face that has come down with any strength. What they preserved instead was something you could hear.

And what they preserved about his people is a habit rather than a boast. The Prophet ﷺ said of them: the Ash'ariyyun, when their provisions run low on a journey or food runs short for their families in Madina, gather whatever they have into one cloth and divide it between them equally. Then he added: 'They are of me and I am of them.'

Hold that picture, because it is the background to the whole of his life. He came from a clan whose distinguishing mark was that they pooled what little they had and shared it out by measure, so that no man ate better than his neighbour. He would later govern a province, and he would be judged by exactly that standard.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Partnership, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari — the Ash'ariyyun and the shared cloth
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Partnership; his name and tribe as given throughout Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Neither a Makkan nor a man of Madina
layers.content:
He belonged to neither of the two groups the early histories are built around. He was not a Muhajir of Quraysh and not an Ansari of Madina. He came from outside — from a tribe in the south that heard about the Prophet ﷺ at a distance and travelled towards him.

Abu Musa himself narrates the moment his party reached Madina, when the Prophet ﷺ told them they had two emigrations rather than one. Reports differ on his own route: some place him among those who went to Abyssinia and came on from there, others bring him directly from Yemen by sea. The histories do not settle it, and there is no need to pretend they do.

What is not in doubt is the timing and the poverty. He and his people arrived as newcomers into a city already full, with no property and no clan of their own to lean on — which is why the report about the shared cloth exists at all.

And then, having crossed all that distance to reach the Prophet ﷺ, he was sent back the way he came. The Prophet ﷺ dispatched him to Yemen to teach, alongside Mu'adh ibn Jabal, each of them to a district.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari — 'you have two emigrations'
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari; the dispatch to Yemen with Mu'adh ibn Jabal in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: 'Make it easy and do not make it hard'
layers.content:
Two sentences went with him to Yemen: make it easy and do not make it hard, give good news and do not drive people away. He was being sent to teach a population that had never met the Prophet ﷺ, and the instruction he was given was not about doctrine. It was about how a teacher should feel to sit in front of.

The other thing said to him was about his voice. 'Abu Musa, you have been given one of the mizmars of the family of Dawud.' The comparison is to the prophet whose recitation the mountains and birds are described as answering.

The version that stays with you is what surrounded it. The Prophet ﷺ told him: if you had seen me last night, I was standing and listening to your recitation. Abu Musa's reply was not thanks. It was, had I known you were listening, I would have made it more beautiful for you.

He was near enough to the household to be a witness to it. It is Abu Musa who reports the Prophet ﷺ in his final illness saying, 'Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer.' And it is Abu Musa who said of another Companion: 'I saw the Prophet ﷺ, and I only saw Ibn Mas'ud as part of his family.'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari — the mizmars of the family of Dawud; the night exchange in Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an; Sahih Muslim; the final-illness report narrated from Abu Musa through his son Abu Burda, and the words about Ibn Mas'ud narrated through Abu Ishaq — both in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: He spoke first at Adhruh, and lost everything
layers.content:
Twice he was put in a position and did not come out of it well, and the sources record both without softening them.

The small one first. As governor he gave 'Umar's wife 'Atika a carpet, a cubit by a span. 'Umar saw it, asked where it came from, struck her on the head with it, and sent for Abu Musa. 'What made you give something to my wives?' Then he hit him with it too: 'Take it. We have no need of it.' Abu Musa said only, 'Do not be hasty, Amir al-Mu'minin.' He did not argue his intentions. He took the correction.

The large one destroyed his name. At Siffin, in Safar 37 AH, when the Syrians raised copies of the Qur'an — a device Ibn Sa'd attributes to 'Amr ibn al-'As — the fighting stopped and arbitration was agreed. Abu Musa was 'Ali's arbiter. 'Amr was Mu'awiya's.

They met at Adhruh in Sha'ban 38 AH, in front of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Umar and other Companions. 'Amr had Abu Musa speak first. Abu Musa spoke and dismissed 'Ali. Then 'Amr spoke, affirmed Mu'awiya, and gave him allegiance. Ibn Sa'd's next line is flat: 'The people parted on that.'

He was outmanoeuvred in public, and the ummah paid for it.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the carpet narrated from Ibn 'Umar through 'Abdullah ibn Waqid, and the account of Siffin and the arbitration at Adhruh in Ibn Sa'd's own narrative

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: He saw 'Umar's death and would not write it to him
layers.content:
Before all of that, he governed Basra for 'Umar, and Basra is where his real work sits. He taught the Qur'an there to a city being built out of nothing, and the recitation of Iraq grew from his mouth.

He also spoke up for the people he answered for. Al-Hasan describes the Basra delegation visiting 'Umar in Madina, finding him eating three loaves with oil or a little yoghurt, and being too uncomfortable to eat. It was Abu Musa who pressed the matter until they raised it: the governors need a fixed allowance from the treasury. 'Umar scratched at the ground a while, then allotted it.

And there is a dream. He told Anas ibn Malik that he saw himself taking many paths until only one remained, and it led him up a mountain where the Prophet ﷺ stood at the top with Abu Bakr beside him, and the Prophet ﷺ was gesturing to 'Umar to come up. Abu Musa woke and said, we belong to Allah and to Him we return, the Amir al-Mu'minin has died. He was asked whether he had written to 'Umar about it. He said: 'I would not announce his death to him.'

He knew what he had seen. He would not be the one to put it in a letter.

He outlived 'Ali. Reports differ on the year and the place of his death. What the ummah kept from him came down largely through his son Abu Burda: a body of narration, and a way of reciting.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the Basra delegation narrated from al-Hasan through Jarir ibn Hazim, and the dream narrated from Anas ibn Malik through Thabit al-Bunani

quiz.prompt: What habit of the Ash'ariyyun did the Prophet ﷺ praise, before saying 'they are of me and I am of them'?

options.text: They never asked anyone for anything
They pooled their remaining food in one cloth and divided it equally
They fasted every Monday and Thursday
They were the first tribe to accept Islam entirely

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Partnership, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: The detail that carries it is 'equally'. Not the strongest taking most, not the generous one giving his away. Measured out, so that nobody could tell who had arrived with more.

quiz.prompt: What instruction did the Prophet ﷺ give Abu Musa and Mu'adh ibn Jabal when sending them to teach in Yemen?

options.text: Collect the zakat before teaching anything
Make it easy and do not make it hard; give good news and do not drive people away
Do not accept any gift from the people of Yemen
Teach only those who ask you three times

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was sent to people with no prior contact with the Prophet ﷺ, and the brief he was given was about manner rather than content. How the teaching felt was part of the teaching.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu Musa say when the Prophet ﷺ told him he had been standing and listening to his recitation the night before?

options.text: 'I did not think anyone was awake'
'Then I will never recite aloud again'
'Had I known you were listening, I would have made it more beautiful for you'
'It was not my voice you heard'

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had a reserve he had not spent. Not showmanship — he was reciting alone in the night. But for that listener he would have found something more.

quiz.prompt: What happened at the arbitration meeting at Adhruh in Sha'ban 38 AH?

options.text: Both arbiters refused to speak and the matter was dropped
'Amr had Abu Musa speak first; Abu Musa dismissed 'Ali, and 'Amr then affirmed Mu'awiya
The Companions present overruled both arbiters
Abu Musa affirmed 'Ali and 'Amr accepted it

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Ibn 'Umar were in the room. Ibn Sa'd records the sequence and then one sentence: the people parted on that.

quiz.prompt: After dreaming that the Prophet ﷺ was calling 'Umar up the mountain, what did Abu Musa refuse to do?

options.text: Return to Basra
Tell anyone about the dream at all
Write to 'Umar about it, saying he would not announce his death to him
Continue as governor

quiz.citation: Narrated from Anas ibn Malik through Thabit al-Bunani — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was certain enough to say the words 'we belong to Allah and to Him we return' out loud. And still he would not be the hand that delivered it.

quiz.prompt: Abu Musa had a reserve of beauty in his recitation he only wished he had spent for the right listener. Where do you hold something back?

options.text: I give my best effort where it will be seen
I hold back out of self-protection more than calculation
I have no reserve left; everything goes out at once
I save my best for the people closest to me and manage elsewhere

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was alone in the dark when it happened. His regret was not that he had been careless, but that he had been unaware of the audience.

quiz.prompt: Struck with the carpet, he said only 'do not be hasty' and took the correction. How do you receive being corrected in front of others?

options.text: I explain my intentions immediately, which usually makes it worse
I go quiet and carry the resentment for a long time
I can accept the substance but not the manner
I would rather be corrected publicly than privately talked about

quiz.citation: Narrated from Ibn 'Umar through 'Abdullah ibn Waqid — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was a serving governor and a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ. He had every standing to object, and the only thing he asked for was that 'Umar slow down.

quiz.prompt: At Adhruh he was outmanoeuvred by someone shrewder, in front of witnesses, with consequences he could not undo. What do you do with a mistake that cannot be repaired?

options.text: I rehearse it at night years later
I have made peace with one and not with the others
I keep looking for the version where it was not my fault
I have decided the repair is in what I do next, not in going back

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The books keep his failure in and keep his narrations in. A man is not the single worst afternoon of his life, and the sources did not treat him as though he were.

quiz.prompt: The Basra delegation could not bring themselves to eat 'Umar's food, and Abu Musa was the one who raised the awkward subject of money. Are you the one who says the uncomfortable thing?

options.text: Usually, and it has cost me
Never — I wait for someone braver
Only when it is on behalf of other people
I raise it badly and too late

quiz.citation: Narrated from al-Hasan through Jarir ibn Hazim — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'Umar's answer was a question: are you not content with what I am content with for myself. And then he scratched the ground, thought, and gave them the allowance anyway.

quiz.prompt: He was neither Muhajir nor Ansari — an outsider who travelled a long way in. When have you been the newcomer in a place with its own history?

options.text: Often, and I have learned to sit at the back first
It made me work twice as hard to be taken seriously
I still feel like a guest somewhere I have been for years
I have never had to; I am not sure I would manage it

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He arrived with no property and no clan in the city, and he ended up governing a province and teaching a school of recitation that outlasted him.
